name: Nebius Group

profile.site: Former Regions Lakeshore Operations Center plus adjoining parcels at 250 and 260 Milan Parkway and 2500 Venice Road, approximately 75 to 80 acres, acquired for about 90 million dollars in transactions closing 2025-09-30 through affiliate Alabama ADC Holdings LLC
profile.phases: Two phases; second 200 MW phase targeted fall 2028

profile.reading: Nebius' Birmingham AI Factory, facility codes BHM01 and DCFL BHM01, sits at 201 Milan Parkway in the Oxmoor Corporate Park, Birmingham, Alabama 35211. Per Data Center Dynamics trade press coverage, the site comprises the former Regions Lakeshore Operations Center plus adjoining parcels at 250 and 260 Milan Parkway and 2500 Venice Road, totaling roughly 75 to 80 acres, acquired for approximately 90 million dollars in transactions that closed September 30, 2025 through an affiliate, Alabama ADC Holdings LLC. The project is planned in two phases, with a second 200 megawatt phase targeted for fall 2028. Local news outlets WBHM and BirminghamWatch, citing Birmingham city proceedings, report a total planned capacity of 300 megawatts, though this figure has not been published directly by Nebius itself and is recorded here as reported by secondary sources pending an operator confirmed figure. The facility's design is modeled on Nebius' own 75 megawatt Mantsala, Finland data center. Power for the site comes from Alabama Power, and general contracting is being handled by Hoar Construction. The Birmingham city attorney determined in April 2026 that the project's switching station and substation did not require separate city approval. A residents' class action lawsuit was filed May 13, 2026 and amended May 25, 2026, naming Nebius, Hoar Construction, the City of Birmingham, and Raeden LLC and affiliates as defendants. Nebius Group is an Amsterdam headquartered, Nasdaq listed AI infrastructure company that emerged from the restructuring of Yandex's international assets, building large scale GPU compute campuses, or AI factories, for AI training and inference workloads. This Birmingham site is one of several such facilities the company is developing in the United States and Europe. Public radio station WBHM, in coverage of a since fizzled resident challenge to the project, reports the 300 megawatt figure breaks down as a 100 megawatt Phase I with a 200 megawatt Phase II by 2028, consistent with the two phase structure reported elsewhere. WBHM reports the completed facility is projected to use approximately 2.6 billion kilowatt hours of electricity annually, roughly double Birmingham's total residential electricity consumption, and that Nebius plans a closed loop cooling system using 56 industrial chillers rather than water intensive evaporative cooling, backed by four 3 megawatt diesel generators with 24,000 gallon fuel tanks each for emergency shutdowns, plus 32 temporary natural gas and diesel generators planned to run only during a 3 to 6 month commissioning period. Birmingham adopted a data center moratorium on March 3, 2026, but this project was grandfathered in because building permits had already been filed. Mayor Randall Woodfin, per WBHM, said the city had been sued twice in similar situations and lost both times over comparable grandfathering disputes, explaining the city's posture toward this project. More than 100 residents attended March 26, 2026 hearings raising noise, water use, property value, and transparency concerns, with nearby institutions including Oxmoor Valley Elementary, Spring Valley School, the Greater Birmingham Humane Society, and United Way facilities cited as potentially affected neighbors.

reading:
Nebius Group is an AI cloud company listed on Nasdaq as NBIS and headquartered in Amsterdam. It exists in its present form because Yandex sold its Russian domestic business in 2024 and the international entity that remained was renamed Nebius. It sells GPU capacity for AI training and inference rather than colocation space, operates or leases capacity in Finland, the United Kingdom, France, Israel, Iceland and the United States, and has said it is targeting 2.5 GW of contracted capacity by the end of 2026.

The one American row is BHM01 in Birmingham, Alabama, and it is among the better documented projects in this registry because residents took the city to court over it. A Nebius affiliate, Alabama ADC Holdings LLC, closed on about 79.3 acres in the Oxmoor Corporate Park area off Lakeshore Parkway on 30 September 2025 for 90 million dollars, buying non contiguous parcels that include the former Regions Lakeshore Operations Center at 201 Milan Parkway together with 250 and 260 Milan Parkway and 2500 Venice Road, from Regions Bank, U.S. Steel and the UAB Research Foundation. The Milan Parkway building is slated for demolition. Court filings describe BHM01 as a 300 MW hyperscale campus built in two phases, 100 MW first and 200 MW after, with construction starting in spring 2026 and full build out by 2028, and record six project permits carrying fees totalling about 34.9 million dollars.

The local record is the substance of this entry. Birmingham published notice of an intended data centre ordinance on 16 December 2025, a permit for this project was requested on 7 January 2026, and the city adopted a moratorium on 3 March 2026. BHM01 was treated as exempt because its approval process had begun before the moratorium was declared. Phase two building permits were filed on 10 April 2026 and demolition and electrical permits were issued at the end of that month. A class action was filed on 13 May 2026 and amended on 25 May, alleging that the city and the developers coordinated to outrun the moratorium and that the land was marked up from an arm's length 20 million dollars to roughly 90 million through intermediary entities including Raeden LLC, 201 Milan Birmingham LLC and Lakeshore Data Center LLC. A judge allowed the suit to proceed in July 2026. On 9 June 2026 the City Council approved a data centre ordinance by six votes to three after nearly three hours of public comment, setting a five acre minimum lot size, a 500 foot setback, a prohibition on on site power generation and a closed loop cooling requirement, while removing the special exception step for hyperscale projects, which was the change residents objected to most loudly.

The 300 MW figure describes the project's intended scale as stated in filings. Nebius has not published an IT load for BHM01, and the two numbers should not be treated as the same thing.
